text: Mott dropped his crate. Straw puffed out through the slats. "Do not call me that," Mott said. "I pull half the weight on this berth and you know it."
"Harbourmaster's past seventy and asleep in his tower. He's not hobbling down here on that cane for one box. Leave the old man be," Grell said.

The third count he did properly, against the register, line by line. This took the better part of an hour. He read each entry aloud, found its shelf and its place, laid his finger on it, and ticked it. Harbour dues, first quarter, year of the low tide: present. Warehousing, bonded, east sheds: present. It was dull, careful work, and he was good at it, and the shelves were a testament to that. Not one volume out of order in four years. Not one.

Ivo jumped so hard that he struck his elbow on the doorframe. He said, "Coming, I do apologise, coming," and climbed the stairs, and he couldn't help but count them on the way up. Nineteen. There had always been nineteen.

Below the birch line the ground turned soft and the bracken stood waist high and rust brown. I lost the boot twice in it and found it both times by the broken stems, which lean the way a man was walking for a day or so before they give up and lie flat. I found where he had stopped to eat. I found crumbs of black bread, a twist of greased paper, and a flat stone where he had sat and knocked the mud off his heel. I sat on the same stone for a moment, out of professional courtesy, and ate one of my oatcakes.

I found the pony with the twisted shoe at the end of the horse line. I found the courier a few minutes later. He was sitting on an upturned crate by the fire with his boots off, rubbing his left heel, and I felt an unreasonable satisfaction at being right about the heel.
The gill was narrow and the evening was still, and voices rose to me as clearly as if I had been sitting at the fire. I lay with my cheek against the pine needles and listened.

"Nobody but you?" Brannoch said. "And you are such a lucky man, are you not?" He tucked the bundle under his arm. "But what does it matter now? Who in Varrow will pay most to have this home again, would you say? A merchant? A magistrate? Or some poor little man who counts things for a living, and who cannot sleep tonight for wondering where it went?"

He was young, certainly not yet thirty, with a thick head of dark hair cropped close at the sides and a weathered blue coat worn open over a plain shirt. He had the restless vigour of a man who had never in his life been asked to wait, and he looked Anselm over with frank, unhurried attention, from the polished boots to the silver clasp at the collar, before he spoke.

"I understand perfectly," Anselm said, who understood only that he had just been told something and had not yet decided what. He watched the clerk's eyes go once, quickly, toward the grey bulk of the customs house and then back to the deck boards, and he set the movement aside beside the Captain's careful silence and the junior secretary's careless wine.

They went down together onto the quay. Captain Oduya walked half a step ahead and slightly to Anselm's left, in the position of a man who expects to be required to stand between his guest and something, and Ivo Penn trailed behind them murmuring figures to himself. The smell of the harbour rose to meet them: brine and tar, wet rope, fish going over in the sun, and beneath everything the flat mineral scent of salt. The men at the stalled berth watched them pass. One of them spat, without great conviction, into the water. Captain Oduya looked at him, and he found an urgent reason to return to his barrel.
